courses.description: Maternal mortality and safe motherhood, family planning, newborn and child survival, adolescent health and nutrition programmes in Nigeria.

topics.title: Maternal Health and Safe Motherhood
topics.summary: Maternal mortality measures and causes, the three delays, and effective interventions.

material.heading: Maternal mortality
material.body: Maternal death is the death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of the end of pregnancy from causes related to or aggravated by pregnancy, excluding accidental causes. The maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is maternal deaths per 100,000 live births; Nigeria's MMR is among the world's highest (around 1,000 per 100,000), and Nigeria accounts for over a quarter of global maternal deaths. Direct causes: haemorrhage (especially postpartum — the leading cause), hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia/eclampsia), sepsis, unsafe abortion and obstructed labour; indirect causes include anaemia, malaria and HIV. SDG target 3.1 aims for global MMR < 70 per 100,000 by 2030.

material.heading: Three delays and interventions
material.body: The three delays model (Thaddeus and Maine): delay in deciding to seek care (poor recognition of danger signs, cost, women's autonomy, cultural factors), delay in reaching a facility (transport, distance, roads, insecurity) and delay in receiving adequate care at the facility (staff, supplies, blood, referral). Effective interventions: family planning, focused/positive antenatal care (WHO recommends at least 8 contacts), skilled birth attendance, emergency obstetric care (basic EmONC — parenteral antibiotics, uterotonics, anticonvulsants (MgSO4), manual removal of placenta, removal of retained products, assisted vaginal delivery, newborn resuscitation; comprehensive EmONC adds caesarean section and blood transfusion), active management of the third stage of labour (oxytocin), misoprostol for community PPH prevention, and postnatal care. Maternal death surveillance and response (MPDSR) reviews deaths to prevent recurrence.

topics.title: Family Planning
topics.summary: Benefits, methods and effectiveness, unmet need, and programme approaches.

material.heading: Benefits and methods
material.body: Family planning allows individuals and couples to anticipate and attain their desired number and spacing of children. Benefits: reduced maternal and child deaths (preventing high-risk and closely spaced pregnancies and unsafe abortions), women's empowerment, and demographic benefits. Methods: long-acting reversible contraceptives (LARCs — implants such as Jadelle and Implanon, lasting 3–5 years; copper IUD lasting up to 10–12 years; hormonal IUD), short-acting (injectables — DMPA every 3 months, combined oral pills, progestogen-only pills, condoms), permanent (tubal ligation, vasectomy), emergency contraception (levonorgestrel within 72–120 hours, copper IUD within 5 days), lactational amenorrhoea method (exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, infant < 6 months) and fertility awareness methods. LARCs are the most effective reversible methods (failure < 1%). Condoms are the only method also preventing STIs.

material.heading: Programme issues
material.body: Nigeria's modern contraceptive prevalence rate (mCPR) among married women is low (about 12–15%), with a total fertility rate around 5 and wide regional variation (lowest use in the North-West). Unmet need for family planning is the proportion of women who want to stop or delay childbearing but are not using contraception. Barriers include cultural and religious beliefs, spousal disapproval, myths about side effects and infertility, cost, stock-outs and poor access. Strategies: community-based distribution, task-sharing (CHEWs providing injectables and implants), postpartum family planning, male involvement, engagement of religious leaders, adolescent-friendly services, and integration with immunisation and HIV services. Informed choice and voluntarism are core principles.

topics.title: Newborn Health
topics.summary: Neonatal mortality, essential newborn care, and major causes of newborn deaths.

material.heading: Neonatal mortality
material.body: The neonatal period is the first 28 days of life; the neonatal mortality rate (NMR) is deaths per 1,000 live births — Nigeria's is about 35–40, among the highest in the world, and newborns account for nearly half of under-five deaths. Main causes: prematurity complications, birth asphyxia (intrapartum-related events), and neonatal infections (sepsis, pneumonia, tetanus), plus neonatal jaundice. The perinatal mortality rate counts stillbirths (≥ 28 weeks) and early neonatal deaths (first 7 days) per 1,000 total births. The Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP) targets NMR ≤ 12 by 2030 (SDG 3.2).

material.heading: Essential newborn care
material.body: Essential newborn care includes immediate drying and warming (skin-to-skin contact), clean cord care (chlorhexidine 7.1% gel to the cord stump — adopted in Nigeria to reduce infection), delayed cord clamping (1–3 minutes), early initiation of breastfeeding within 1 hour and exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, eye prophylaxis (tetracycline ointment), vitamin K, birth-dose vaccines, and birth registration. Helping Babies Breathe trains birth attendants in resuscitation within the 'Golden Minute'. Kangaroo mother care (continuous skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding) reduces deaths among low-birth-weight babies. Postnatal home visits in the first week detect danger signs (not feeding, convulsions, fast breathing, chest indrawing, fever or low temperature, jaundice on day 1 or on palms and soles).

topics.title: Child Survival and Nutrition
topics.summary: Under-five mortality, IMCI, growth monitoring, malnutrition and micronutrient programmes.

material.heading: Child survival
material.body: The under-five mortality rate (U5MR, deaths before age 5 per 1,000 live births) in Nigeria is about 100–110, among the highest globally. Major causes after the neonatal period: malaria, pneumonia, diarrhoea, measles and malnutrition (an underlying factor in about 45% of deaths). GOBI-FFF (UNICEF's child survival revolution): Growth monitoring, Oral rehydration, Breastfeeding, Immunisation, Female education, Family spacing and Food supplementation. Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) — and its community version iCCM — classifies sick children by danger signs and colour-coded treatment (pink — urgent referral; yellow — specific treatment; green — home care). Diarrhoea is treated with low-osmolarity ORS and zinc for 10–14 days; pneumonia with amoxicillin dispersible tablets.

material.heading: Nutrition
material.body: Forms of malnutrition: stunting (low height-for-age — chronic; about a third of Nigerian under-fives, among the highest numbers globally), wasting (low weight-for-height — acute), underweight (low weight-for-age), micronutrient deficiencies (vitamin A, iron, iodine, zinc) and overweight. Severe acute malnutrition (SAM): weight-for-height < −3 SD, MUAC < 11.5 cm, or bilateral pitting oedema (kwashiorkor); managed through community management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) with ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) as outpatients, or inpatient stabilisation (F-75, F-100) if complicated. Interventions: exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months, appropriate complementary feeding from 6 months, vitamin A supplementation (6–59 months, every 6 months), iron-folic acid, universal salt iodisation, deworming, growth monitoring and food fortification. The first 1,000 days (conception to age 2) are the critical window.

topics.title: Adolescent and Sexual Health
topics.summary: Adolescent health needs, harmful practices, STIs, and gender-based violence.

material.heading: Adolescents
material.body: Adolescents (10–19 years) form about a quarter of Nigeria's population. Health issues: early marriage and adolescent pregnancy (high in the North-West — girls < 18 face higher risks of obstructed labour, obstetric fistula, eclampsia and death), unsafe abortion, HIV and STIs, mental health problems, substance use (e.g. tramadol, codeine syrup), malnutrition and anaemia, and injuries. Youth-friendly health services are accessible, acceptable, confidential, non-judgemental and appropriately staffed. Comprehensive sexuality education (Family Life and HIV Education in Nigeria) and keeping girls in school delay marriage and pregnancy. The Child Rights Act 2003 sets 18 as the minimum age of marriage, though not domesticated in all states.

material.heading: Harmful practices and GBV
material.body: Female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) involves partial or total removal of external genitalia for non-medical reasons (types I–IV); Nigeria has a large absolute number of women affected; it causes haemorrhage, infection, obstructed labour, fistula and psychological harm, and was banned federally by the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act 2015. Gender-based violence (physical, sexual, emotional and economic) is widespread; survivors need clinical management of rape (within 72 hours: emergency contraception, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, STI prophylaxis, hepatitis B vaccination, psychosocial support, forensic documentation) and referral to Sexual Assault Referral Centres. STI syndromic management treats syndromes (urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, genital ulcer) without lab confirmation, plus partner notification.
